title: How do you find and fix memory leaks in a .NET service?
description: Growing working set, GC diagnostics with dotMemory/PerfView, common leak sources (events, statics, caches), and disposal discipline.

data.text: **Question:** How do you find and fix memory leaks in a .NET service?

Watch for a working set that only climbs (GC memory / #Bytes in all Heaps from dotnet-counters), then **diff heap snapshots** between two points in time in dotMemory or PerfView: objects that keep growing and shouldn't are your leak. The classic .NET culprits: **event handlers never unregistered**, **static collections caching per-request data**, **timers not disposed**, **closures/`async` state machines pinning large objects**, **CancellationTokenRegistrations held**, and **IDisposable never disposed** (HttpClient is the cliché — reuse via IHttpClientFactory). Fixes are usually mechanical once identified: unsubscribe on dispose, use `ConditionalWeakTable`/bounded `ConcurrentDictionary` with eviction for caches, `WeakReference`/`MemoryCache` with size limits, and `await using`/`IAsyncDisposable` for async resources.

items: First signal: dotnet-counters watch — GC Heap Size grows linearly under constant load; Gen2 GC size climbs after every collection
dotMemory/PerfView: take snapshot A, run workload, snapshot B, diff — sort by retained size, look at who roots the survivors
Event-handler leaks: static/singleton subscribing to a scoped object's event — the singleton roots it forever; unsubscribe in Dispose or use WeakEventManager patterns
Static caches without eviction: ConcurrentDictionary keyed by request id — unbounded growth; bound it (size limit + TTL, or MemoryCache)
Timers: System.Timers.Timer/PeriodicTimer held by a disposed scope — dispose them; better, use IHostedService-owned timers
Async leaks: fire-and-forget tasks holding state machines; CancellationTokenSource.CancelRegistrations accumulating
Disposed-but-referenced: a disposed DbContext kept alive by a singleton keeps its change-tracked entities rooted
Finalizers are a symptom, not a fix — an object with a finalizer that leaks also blocks the finalizer thread

Forgetting that 'it gets GC'd eventually' hides slow leaks — Gen2 climbs for days
Adding WeakReference everywhere instead of fixing the ownership model

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Signal: GC heap only grows under steady load; confirm with counter + snapshot diff
Classic culprits: static roots, events, timers, unbounded caches, undisposed disposables
dotnet-counters for signal, dotMemory/PerfView for the culprit graph
Fix ownership, not symptoms: symmetric subscribe/unsubscribe, bounded caches, IHttpClientFactory
data.takeaway: A leak is a reference you didn't know you kept — snapshot the heap twice, diff the survivors, and ask what root is still holding them.
